nodes.label: Ufartes et al. (2020)
nodes.title: De novo mutations in FBRSL1 cause a novel recognizable malformation and intellectual disability syndrome.

nodes.label: Ufartes et al. (2020) reported 3 unrelated children with a recognizable malformation syndrome. All three had impaired intellectual development and/or global developmental delay, delayed speech, autistic behavior, microcephaly, swallowing difficulty, postnatal growth retardation, skeletal abnormalities, camptodactyly/contractures, facial dysmorphism, and respiratory failure that needed ventilation therapy. Heart defects (ASD/PDA, ASD/VSD) were present in 2 patients, as were cleft palate, hearing impairment, and distinctive skin creases. Asplenia and an anal anomaly were each seen in 1 patient.

Ufartes et al. (2020) noted that in 2 of the patients the skin folds were most pronounced right after birth, mainly affected the back rather than the arms and legs, and regressed with age. This pattern differs from congenital symmetric circumferential skin creases syndromes (CSCSC1 and CSCSC2). Other features included a pronounced neck fold, a flat occiput, dysplastic auricles, deep-set eyes, a round face, temporal indentations, contractures of the hands and fingers, and widely spaced teeth.

Trio exome sequencing by Ufartes et al. (2020) found a heterozygous de novo c.487C>T nonsense variant in FBRSL1 in patient 1, producing p.Gln163*. Sanger sequencing confirmed it, and both unaffected parents carried the wild-type sequence. The variant was absent from gnomAD and ExAC, and the transcript escaped nonsense-mediated decay. Pathogenic variants in TUBB, MAPRE2, and AUTS2 were excluded.

Ufartes et al. (2020) initially found no change in the canonical FBRSL1 transcript in patient 2. Manual inspection of intronic reads then revealed a heterozygous de novo 23-bp deletion (c.581_603del), which affects alternative exon 3 of the short N-terminal isoform 3.1 (XM_005266181.4). The deletion causes a frameshift and a premature stop at position 356 that disrupts the DNA translocase domain. Sanger sequencing and RT-PCR confirmed it, and both healthy parents were wild type.

Ufartes et al. (2020) identified a heterozygous c.332G>A nonsense variant in FBRSL1, producing p.Trp111*, in patient 3 by single exome sequencing and reverse phenotyping. The variant was absent from the healthy mother; the father was not available for testing. It was not present in gnomAD or ExAC.

Using RT-PCR and Western blot, Ufartes et al. (2020) validated short N-terminal FBRSL1 isoforms 3.1 (about 66 kDa) and 3.2 (about 55 kDa) alongside the long isoform 1 (about 110 kDa). The short isoforms contain an FtsK DNA translocase domain, and isoform 1 instead contains an AUTS2 domain. All 3 patient variants affect the short isoforms. Isoform 3.1 was expressed mainly in fetal tissues. N-terminal isoforms localized to the cytoplasm and nucleus and associated with centrosomes and kinetochores.

Ufartes et al. (2020) knocked down Fbrsl1 in Xenopus laevis embryos with a splice-blocking morpholino. Knockdown caused reduced craniofacial structures and eyes, cartilage hypoplasia (most severe in the branchial arches), reduced Ncam expression in the brain, and disturbed migration of cranial nerves and motor neurons. Human short isoform 3.1 rescued the craniofacial defects in a dose-dependent manner. Neither the long isoform 1 nor isoform 3.1 carrying p.Gln163* rescued them.

Ufartes et al. (2020) noted that the long FBRSL1 isoform appears tolerant to loss of function (pLI = 0.01), so haploinsufficiency of the long transcripts is unlikely. They suggested two possible mechanisms: haploinsufficiency of short isoform 3.2 causing an imbalance between isoforms, or a dominant-negative effect, because the truncated transcripts escaped nonsense-mediated decay.

Pauli et al. (2021) reviewed 3 unrelated children with truncating FBRSL1 variants. In the newborn period they had breathing failure needing ventilation and feeding difficulties. Later they showed intellectual disability with no active speech, postnatal microcephaly, growth retardation and contractures. Two of the 3 had cleft palate and heart defects (atrial septal defect with patent ductus arteriosus in one, atrial and ventricular septal defects in the other); 1 had asplenia and 1 had anal atresia. The 2 more severely affected children were born with marked skin creases that disappeared during the first year of life.

Pauli et al. (2021) compared the 3 FBRSL1 patients with AUTS2 syndrome using the features of the AUTS2 syndrome severity scoring system. All 3 had short stature, microcephaly, feeding difficulties, intellectual disability, autistic behavior, kyphosis/scoliosis and camptodactyly/contractures. Two of 3 had cerebral palsy/spasticity, high arched eyebrows, epicanthal folds, a deep/broad nasal bridge, a short/upturned philtrum, low-set ears, widely spaced teeth and hearing impairment. None had hypertelorism, ptosis, strabismus or hernias. The authors noted a large overlap with severe AUTS2 syndrome, but with a wider range and higher rate of congenital malformations.

Pauli et al. (2021) noted that all 3 reported patients carried truncating variants in the N-terminal part of FBRSL1 that affect the short N-terminal isoforms: stop variants in 2 patients and a frameshift causing a premature stop codon in 1. By contrast, severe AUTS2 syndrome is linked to variants affecting the AUTS2 C-terminus.

Pauli et al. (2021) summarized Xenopus work in which Fbrsl1 morpholino knockdown caused craniofacial defects with cartilage hypoplasia, smaller brain size, and impaired migration of cranial nerves and motor neurons. A human short N-terminal FBRSL1 isoform rescued the craniofacial defects. Neither a patient-variant version of this isoform nor the long isoform, both lacking the Ftsk domain, rescued them. The authors suggested that mutations in the short N-terminal isoforms cause the developmental phenotype.

Pauli et al. (2021) noted that FBRSL1, like AUTS2, interacts with the Polycomb subcomplexes PRC1.3 and PRC1.5 and competes with AUTS2 for binding to PRC1.5. In HEK293 cells and human fibroblasts, FBRSL1 was found in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm. An N-terminal antibody detected both nuclear and cytoplasmic signal, whereas a C-terminal antibody mainly detected nuclear signal, suggesting that different isoforms have nuclear versus cytoplasmic functions.

Pauli et al. (2021) described a long 19-exon FBRSL1 transcript (NM_001142641.2) and 2 validated short N-terminal isoforms. The short isoforms use an alternative exon 3 that leads to a stop codon; they lack the AUTS2 family domain but include a predicted DNA translocase (Ftsk) domain.

Bukvic et al. (2024) reported a girl, the third child of healthy nonconsanguineous Italian parents (father 46, mother 38 years old at her birth), with threatened miscarriage and poor fetal movements in pregnancy. At term she had low birth weight (2860 g) and length below the 3rd centile, neonatal feeding difficulties due to weak sucking, postnatal growth retardation, bilateral contractures of hands and fingers, bilateral congenital hip dislocation, and irregular bone growth fronts of the long bones; she was initially diagnosed with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita at 4 months of age.

Bukvic et al. (2024) noted that the patient had global developmental delay (head control at 7 months, sitting at 14 months, walking unsupported at 46 months), no active speech and severe intellectual disability at 48 months (developmental quotient 22), and motor stereotypies without autism spectrum disorder. At 48 months she had short stature, low weight, microcephaly, and facial dysmorphism including flat occiput, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, short philtrum, micrognathia, and microstomia with 'whistling mouth'; later examination noted small forehead, bitemporal narrowing, sunken eyes, broad nasal bridge, unusual ears, and thick lips. She also had mild scoliosis, distal limb hypertonia with supinated varus feet, wide-based gait, and cerebral palsy/spasticity; hearing and heart were normal, and brain and spinal MRI at 2 months and 4 years and metabolic studies were normal.

Bukvic et al. (2024) reported that at 46 months of age the patient developed epilepsy with daily drop tonic seizures and later myoclonic absences; ictal EEG showed a high-voltage slow wave followed by voltage attenuation and interictal EEG showed frontocentral spikes and spike-and-wave complexes and 2-Hz diffuse spike-and-wave complexes. Epilepsy, stereotypies, hip dislocation, and mastication problems were noted as features not previously reported in FBRSL1 patients, whereas respiratory insufficiency, cleft palate, heart defects, and hearing impairment reported by Ufartes et al. (2020) were absent.

In the Italian girl, Bukvic et al. (2024) identified by trio clinical exome sequencing a de novo heterozygous 1-bp duplication in exon 2 of the FBRSL1 gene (c.371dupC, NM_001142641.2), causing a frameshift and premature stop codon (p.Cys125Leufs*7) predicted to yield a 131-amino acid protein instead of 1045 residues; the variant was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and absent from the parents. No other variants explaining the phenotype were found.

Bukvic et al. (2024) found by SNP array in the patient a paternally inherited approximately 530-kb duplication at 7p11.2 and two maternally inherited duplications at 16p13.11 (about 470 kb and 1.1 Mb), all classified as variants of uncertain significance; STITCH analysis found no interactions attributable to these duplications that could be linked to the phenotype.

Bukvic et al. (2024) found that genome-wide DNA methylation analysis (EpiSign) of the patient's peripheral blood showed a profile similar to controls for all episignatures tested, including the PRC2 episignature (MVP score of zero); FBRSL1 or PRC1.5 episignatures are undefined.

Bukvic et al. (2024) used in silico modeling of the truncated 131-residue FBRSL1 protein and predicted a self-binding domain (residues 81 to 93) and 2 nuclear localization signals; they hypothesized that the truncated protein could localize to the nucleus and inactivate wildtype FBRSL1, suggesting a possible dominant-negative effect.

Bukvic et al. (2024) reported that the patient's seizures initially responded well to valproic acid but relapsed months later, with better but incomplete control after addition of ethosuximide and rufinamide. A percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy was placed at 6 years for feeding difficulties and poor weight gain, and with multidisciplinary rehabilitation including augmentative and alternative communication she became able to sit and stand independently, walk with minimal support, and communicate basic needs.
Xu et al. (2026) described a patient with neurodevelopmental delay, epilepsy, congenital heart disease, and facial dysmorphism.

In a patient with neurodevelopmental delay, epilepsy, congenital heart disease, and facial dysmorphism, Xu et al. (2026) identified a de novo truncating variant in the FBRSL1 gene, p.Ala128Cysfs*5, by whole-exome sequencing.

Xu et al. (2026) analyzed 4 patients with FBRSL1 variants and described an emerging syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by microcephaly, global developmental delay, autism, facial dysmorphism, and skeletal contractures.
Xu et al. (2026) found that fbrsl1 knockdown in zebrafish recapitulated neurodevelopmental abnormalities, epileptiform discharges, and cardiac dysfunction, consistent with the patient's phenotype.

Xu et al. (2026) found that FBRSL1 is highly expressed in the developing brain and heart, and single-cell RNA sequencing showed high expression in neural progenitors of 1-month-old organoids, suggesting a vital role in neurodevelopment.
